book: 288 - Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas

chapters.relation: Hamilton reads the pick-up-artist 'Game' (Mystery, Style, negs, peacocking, the Alpha frame) against Aristotle's great-souled magnanimous man, arguing that the jerk and the PUA succeed because they inadvertently mimic the Megalopsuche's self-containment and indifference to others' approval. He contends the ethical route is to genuinely acquire that character through habituation ('we become brave by acting bravely') rather than fake it, so the nice guy's supplication fails while true magnanimity requires the full virtues. He then uses Aristotle's three grades of friendship (utility, pleasure, and the highest disinterested philia) to argue that erotic relationships can rise to real friendship only where partners are equals, citing When Harry Met Sally on whether men and women can be friends.

Terjesen defines a 'real date' as a shared intention to try out romantic possibility, using Abelard's claim that intention (not behavior) determines the nature of an act to show that identical activities are or aren't dates depending on mutual intent. He then invokes Russell's argument-from-analogy account of knowing other minds to explain how daters 'mind-read' each other's intentions, and notes this yields only probable conclusions, generating an infinite regress ('I know that you know...') that only 'the Talk' resolves. He cites Hume's problem of induction as the deeper reason analogical inference can never be certain, and uses the Friends 'Mayor of the Friend Zone' gag and Ross and Rachel to argue the Friend Zone is a step toward, not a trap against, committed relationships.

Brown and Tien build a 'Kantian Gate' from Kant's Formula of Universal Law: you should date only if you wouldn't mind your dates acting on your own dating maxim, which bars the manipulative, deceptive, or coercive dater while permitting many ends. For those who pass the gate, they recommend pursuing Csikszentmihalyi's 'flow' and the Zhuangzi's cultivated spontaneity, describing a two-part self-cultivation (purging debilitating social programming via 'forgetting' and xinzhai, then training to act in accord with the Dao) so one can 'be in the moment' and get truly lucky on a first date. They apply the seven elements of flow directly to dating conversation, eye contact, and feedback.

Brinkman uses the Second Life case of Ric and Janet (whose avatars Dutch and Tenaj dated and 'married' virtually before the couple left their spouses) to ask ontological questions about whether virtual dating and virtual cheating are real. Drawing on Huizinga's Homo Ludens, he argues dating is itself pervaded by the 'play-spirit' (the magic circle, the dating script, secrecy, rapture) and that virtual worlds and dating both breed 'spoilsports': he maps virtual-world 'griefers' and pick-up-artist 'wizards' and 'script kiddies' (via Strauss's The Game) onto Huizinga's cheater/spoilsport distinction, concluding that PUAs who treat targets as game pieces commit a moral transgression against ludus even when they don't lie, and that Ric really was cheating.

Silber uses his own Match.com romance with Karin to argue that virtual 'meeting' differs phenomenologically from face-to-face meeting, which Buber's I-Thou (vs I-It) makes into a whole-being encounter that online traces and aspects cannot supply, invoking 'all real living is meeting.' He treats the dating market as a site of Kantian danger, contrasting price with the dignity of persons in the kingdom of ends, and warns that the market's efficiency threatens objectification and commodification. He then deploys Sartre's bad faith, facticity and transcendence, and 'existence precedes essence' to diagnose online self-misrepresentation (lying about height, age, photos) as inauthenticity, while briefly setting Derrida's 'nothing outside the text' against Plato's Phaedrus preference for speech over writing.

Naar and Masala defend the 'Secret Underground Internet Seduction Community' by grounding it in Darwinian sexual selection (the peacock's tail, mate value, women prioritizing status and men prioritizing youth/beauty) and an Aristotelian ideal of happiness as excellence: they read the community's aim of becoming a well-rounded seducer as cultivating virtue and social/emotional 'mating intelligence' that yields eudaimonic fulfillment. Against the Kantian objection that seduction training uses women merely as means, they offer a consequentialist and 'deflationist' reply that deception and manipulation already pervade ordinary courtship (makeup, lying about age), so raising one's mate value is morally neutral, and they extend the point to women's active and passive seduction strategies (Cleopatra, groupies).

Colyvan applies mathematics and game theory to mating: the 'secretary problem' yields the optimal strategy of dating and rejecting the first n/e (~37%) of candidates then taking the next best, and Rousseau's stag hunt models monogamy as cooperation (hunt stag = stay faithful) tempted by defection (hunt hare = an affair), with the prisoner's dilemma showing why individual rationality can undermine the Pareto-optimal cooperative outcome. He argues that iterated games and tit-for-tat strategies, plus the 'shadow of the future' and public commitments like weddings, make faithfulness explicable purely by narrow self-interest, quoting Hume on reciprocal service, and suggests love and ethics themselves may be useful fictions layered over the game.

Clark uses Barry Schwartz's Paradox of Choice and the characters of Sex and the City to argue that too much dating choice turns people into unhappy 'maximizers' who seek the absolute best, rather than 'satisficers' content with the merely excellent. She traces how Charlotte, Miranda, Carrie, Big, and Samantha each attain their maximized 'ideal' mate (Trey, Robert Leeds, Petrovsky/Big, Richard Wright) and find it hollow, only becoming happy when they 'settle' for a reciprocal partner (Harry, Steve, John, Smith) after the post-9/11 shift in the series' mood. She frames maximizing as clinically narcissistic (choosing a mate as a mirror of oneself) and invokes Plato to warn that trying to make the ideal real yields only disappointment.

holes.name: Peter Abelard
holes.what: Twelfth-century medieval logician and ethicist who held that the morality of an act is determined by the agent's intention (consent) rather than the outward behavior.
holes.why: Chapter 23 rests its whole definition of a 'real date' on Abelard's intention-based ethics from his Ethics, and no existing taxonomy philosopher covers this intention-determines-the-act thesis.

holes.name: Johan Huizinga
holes.what: Dutch cultural historian and theorist of play whose Homo Ludens argues that culture arises in and through play, defining the 'magic circle' and the cheater/spoilsport distinction.
holes.why: Chapter 26's entire ludic analysis of dating and virtual worlds is built on Huizinga's theory of play, the magic circle, and spoilsports, and no existing taxonomy philosopher or concept captures the philosophy of play.

holes.name: Play and the Magic Circle
holes.what: Huizinga's account of play as a free, absorbing activity set apart in its own bounded time and space (the 'magic circle') with its own rules, distinct from ordinary serious life.
holes.why: Chapter 26 applies the magic circle and the play-spirit directly to the dating script and to Second Life, and the taxonomy has no concept for the philosophy of play or games.

holes.name: The Paradox of Choice (maximizers vs satisficers)
holes.what: Barry Schwartz's thesis that an overload of options tends to reduce satisfaction, distinguishing 'maximizers' who seek the absolute best from 'satisficers' content with the good enough.
holes.why: Chapter 31's central argument that abundant dating choice makes people unhappy maximizers is organized entirely around Schwartz's maximizer/satisficer distinction, which no existing taxonomy concept expresses.
